# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Midterm 1, 2025 (past paper)

**1.** Of 50 surveyed drivers, 30 own an electric car, and 12 of the electric
car owners charge at work. What percentage of electric car owners charge at
work?

**2.** Write the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean
commute time differs from 30 minutes, and state what a p-value of 0.03 means
at the 5% level.

**3.** A grouped summary computes the mean score for each of 4 sections of a
course with 120 students. How many rows does the result have?
materials.notes.md:
# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Lecture notes

## §1 Conditional probability

§1.1 P(A | B) is read "the probability of A among B". It answers: of the
cases in group B, what share are also in A?

§1.2 Compute it as (number of cases in both A and B) divided by (number of
cases in B). The denominator is the reference group B, not the whole sample.

§1.3 The order matters. P(A | B) and P(B | A) usually differ because they use
different reference groups. Before computing, decide which group the question
restricts you to; that group is the denominator.

§1.4 Assume every case is equally weighted and the reference group is not
empty.

## §2 Two-way tables

§2.1 A two-way table counts cases by two categorical variables at once, one in
the rows and one in the columns, with row totals and column totals.

§2.2 A row percentage divides a cell by its row total; a column percentage
divides a cell by its column total. Choosing row versus column percentages is
the same decision as choosing the reference group in §1.2.

§2.3 Row percentages in one row add to 100%; column percentages in one column
add to 100%. Percentages across a row of column percentages need not.

## §3 Grouped summaries

§3.1 A grouped summary splits the cases by a categorical variable and computes
one summary value (such as a mean or a count) per group.

§3.2 The result has one row per non-empty group, not one row per original case.

§3.3 Compare groups using the same summary; do not compare a group mean with a
group total.

Current as of this week. This outline replaces earlier versions.

# STAT 110 (synthetic) — Practice set A (T1 conditional probability)

Answer keys are in practice-key.md. Use the outline's reporting rule.

**Q1.** A class has 40 students. 25 of them commute. 10 of the commuters cycle
to campus. What percentage of commuters cycle?

**Q2.** A company has 60 employees. 24 of them work remotely. 6 of the remote
workers are trainees. What percentage of remote workers are trainees?

**Q3.** A club has 30 members. 12 of them are seniors. 4 of the seniors
volunteer at events. What percentage of seniors volunteer?

**Q4.** A store had 45 shoppers today. 20 of them ordered online. 9 of the
online shoppers returned an item. What percentage of online shoppers returned
an item?

responses.1:
I’ll check your course files for conditional probability, explain it from those materials, and start a short progress file for next time.

The local file listing is taking longer than expected. I’m waiting to read your materials so the explanation stays within your course’s coverage.

According to your [lecture notes, §1](materials/notes.md), **conditional probability means “the probability of A among B.”** You restrict your attention to group B, then ask what share also belongs to A.

\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{\text{number in both A and B}}{\text{number in B}}
\]

The key is the **reference group**: the group after the vertical bar supplies the denominator, rather than the whole sample. Your notes assume equally weighted cases and a nonempty reference group.

Order matters: “cycle among commuters” uses all commuters as the reference group; “commute among cyclists” uses all cyclists. These usually give different results.

Your [midterm outline](materials/outline.md) requires answers as percentages rounded to **one decimal place**, with the reference group named.

Try **Practice Q1**: A class has 40 students. Of these, 25 commute, and 10 of the commuters cycle to campus. What percentage of commuters cycle?

**Which group is your denominator, and what percentage do you get?**

I’ve started [progress.md](progress.md). Your understanding hasn’t been assessed yet; we’ll build evidence from your attempts.
responses.2:
I’ll record your attempt and the denominator choice we need to work on in your progress file.

Your arithmetic is correct, but the denominator needs changing. The question asks **“what percentage of commuters cycle?”**, so the reference group is the **25 commuters**. The order in which the numbers appear doesn’t determine the denominator ([Notes §1.2–1.3](materials/notes.md)).

Divide the 10 commuters who cycle by the 25 commuters: **40.0% of commuters cycle**.

Your calculation instead tells us that **25.0% of all students are commuters who cycle**.

To check your understanding: **Which words in Q1 tell you to use 25 as the denominator?**
responses.3:
I’ll record Q2 as an answer provided on request, rather than an independent attempt.

**25.0% of remote workers are trainees.** Divide the 6 remote trainees by the 24 remote workers, then multiply by 100.

Why is the denominator 24 rather than 60?
responses.4:
I’ll record Q3 as correct without a hint, including your explanation of the reference group.

Correct: **33.3% of seniors volunteer at events.** You chose the right denominator, explained why, and followed the reporting rule.

That’s one correct independent application—evidence of progress, though we haven’t established consistency yet.

Try **Q4**: A store had 45 shoppers. Of these, 20 ordered online, and 9 of the online shoppers returned an item. **What percentage of online shoppers returned an item, and why did you choose that denominator?**
responses.5:
I’ll record Q4 as your second correct independent application and note what we still need to check.

Correct: **45.0% of online shoppers returned an item**, using the 20 online shoppers as the denominator.

You’ve now answered two similar questions correctly without hints. That supports understanding the basic calculation and reference group. We haven’t yet checked whether you can handle reversed conditions—the point in Notes §1.3—or remember this later, so I wouldn’t call it mastered yet.

Let’s check: If Q4 instead asked, **“What percentage of shoppers who returned an item ordered online?”**, which group would be the denominator? Does Q4 give you that group’s total?
responses.6:

I’ll record that you correctly handled the reversed condition and identified the missing information.

Correct. **All volunteers** are the reference group, and their total is missing. With that total, you would divide 4 by it and convert to a percentage.

This shows you can reason about a reversed condition and recognize insufficient information. Along with Q3 and Q4, that supports a solid basic understanding; retention still needs checking later. I’ve updated your progress file.

Updated: 2026-11-14. Midterm next week.

## Preferences
Use only course files; flag missing coverage. No practice answers before an attempt unless requested. Check understanding after explanations. Assess learning conservatively.

## Sources and rules
- Read: materials/outline.md, notes.md, practice.md.
- Report percentages to one decimal place and name the reference group.
